bible_refs.note: lemma: τήν τε γὰρ ἐπιθυμίαν οὐκ ᾔδειν ... πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν (7:7-8a), exact wording
Οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις, quoted by Paul inside Romans 7:7 (also Deuteronomy 5:21)
lemma: Χωρὶς γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία νεκρά (7:8b)
ἐζηκέναι χωρὶς νόμου ποτέ ... ἀναβιῶναι ... τεθνάναι; 'I died' is 7:10a
Cyril's form ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς, καὶ μὴ ποιήσας, δαρήσεται ὀλίγας; Luke reads ὁ δὲ μὴ γνούς, ποιήσας δὲ ἄξια πληγῶν, δαρήσεται ὀλίγας

choices.why: ἐπιθυμία is rendered 'covetous desire' inside the Romans lemma, to keep the link with 'You shall not covet', and 'desire(s)' in Cyril's own comment.
ἐπεβούλευσεν ('plotted against') is rendered 'turned against us'; the object is implied.

pass_a_gloss: [Cont. from u04-open: someone taking a torch] set (ἔστησε) [it] at the crossroads (τριόδοις), making manifest (ἐμφανῆ καθιστάς) to those there the things in between (τὰ μεταξύ), not that they might stumble (περιπταίωσιν) on them again, but rather that they might step over (ὑπερφέροιντο) and be rid (ἀπαλλάττοιντο) of the harm (κακοῦ). Did the light (φῶς) then wrong (ἠδίκησε) [them], because it showed (παρέδειξε) what pains (τὸ λυποῦν)? Or rather we say that it worked in them very great benefit (ὄνησιν) and made [them] safer (ἀσφαλεστέρους)? But I think this is unclear (ἀσυμφανές) to no one. When then, being sinners (ἁμαρτωλοί), stumbling on very many charges (ἐγκλήμασι), we knew (ἐγνώκαμεν) sin (ἁμαρτίαν) through the law (νόμου), the law would not reasonably be thought or called sin, far from it, but rather indicative (παραδεικτικός) of sin, as I said. [Lemma Rom 7:7-8a] For I would not have known desire (ἐπιθυμίαν) unless the law said 'you shall not desire'; taking occasion (ἀφορμήν) through the commandment (ἐντολῆς) sin worked in me every desire. And he brings in the powerlessness/weakness (ἀδρανές) of our nature (φύσεως): that the law given for benefit plotted against (ἐπεβούλευσεν) unexpectedly (ἀδοκήτως), as the light of the sun to those weak of eye. When then he says the commandment in a way became occasion for the desires, let no one think he accuses (κατηγορεῖν) the law, but rather cries out against (κατακεκραγέναι) the weakness (ἀσθενείας) in us; whereas we should have been checked (ἀνακόπτεσθαι) through the law, through these [we are] spurred (παροτρυνομένους) to worse. For the mind (διάνοια) of man always is sick (νοσεῖ) with love-of-empty (φιλόκενον) toward desires; and the one doing the desires lives as he wills, untroubled (ἀνενόχλητος); the one checking them receives a fiercer (ἀγριωτέραν) onset (ἔφοδον) of passions (παθῶν); and of things at hand (προχείρων) none desires, but what one is prevented (κωλύεται) from, he desires. Hence the law having forbidden the harmful (βλάπτον), it became occasion to the weaker of desiring it more. [Lemma Rom 7:8b] For apart from law sin [is] dead (νεκρά). For if there were not laid down, he says, the law condemning (καταδικάζων) the way of wickedness (φαυλότητος), evil would become powerless (ἀδρανές); for it is all but (μονονουχί) provoked (κατερεθίζεται) to strength through the law, and more slackly (ῥᾳθυμότερον) for some will lie the goad (κέντρον) of pleasure (ἡδονῆς), no one rebuking (ἐπιτιμῶντος) it; and all but blunted (ἀπαμβλύνεται), bewitched (γοητευόμενον) by the breadth (πλάτει) of license (ἐξουσίας); for where there is nothing at all resisting (ἀντιστατοῦν), there surely the contentiousness (φιλόνεικον) also is idle (ἀργεῖ). Dead therefore is sin when law does not declare (διαγορεύοντος) what is to be done. The mystagogue (μυσταγωγός) says he lived once without law; then the commandment coming, sin revived (ἀναβιῶναι), but he himself died, he insists (διισχυρίζεται). He shapes (σχηματίζει) the speech in these things upon himself; but I think he wishes to show something such: under justice/penalty (ὑπὸ δίκην) admittedly is also sinning in ignorance (ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ πλημμελεῖν); but that heavier (φορτικωτέρα) for those who know will be the punishment (κόλασις), the Saviour (Σωτήρ) has fully assured (πεπληροφόρηκεν) saying: The one knowing the will of his lord and not doing, will be beaten (δαρήσεται) many; but the one not knowing and not doing, will be beaten few. Therefore admittedly better to sin in ignorance than in knowledge (εἰδήσει) of laws. But if someone came under law, having once lived the life outside law, then having chosen (ᾑρημένος) to disregard (ἀφειδεῖν) the decrees (τεθεσπισμένων), was convicted (ἥλω) on an indictment (γραφῇ) of sin and fell [cont. u04-rem-mid: under penalty].
pass_b_english: […] set it up at the crossroads, and so made plain to those on the road what lay in their path, not so that they would stumble over these things again, but rather so that they might step over them and escape the harm. Did the light, then, do them wrong because it showed them what was hurting them? Or shall we say instead that it did them the greatest possible good and made them safer? This, I think, is clear to everyone.

So when we, who were sinners and stumbled into a great many offenses, came to know sin through the law, the law could not reasonably be thought or called sin, far from it. Rather, as I said, it is what points sin out.

“For I would not have known covetous desire if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, seizing an occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire” (Romans 7:7–8; Exodus 20:17). Here he also brings in the weakness of our nature: the law, given for our benefit, turned against us when no one expected it, as the light of the sun does to those whose eyes are weak. So when he says that the commandment in a way became an occasion for desires, let no one suppose that he is accusing the law. He is rather crying out against the weakness in us, since we, who ought to have been held back by the law, are spurred on by these very things toward what is worse.

For the human mind is always sick with a love of empty things that draws it toward desires. The one who carries out his desires lives as he pleases and is left untroubled; but the one who checks them meets a fiercer onslaught of the passions. No one desires what lies ready to hand; what a person is forbidden, that he desires. So when the law forbade what does harm, it became for the weaker an occasion to desire that very thing all the more.

“For apart from the law sin is dead” (Romans 7:8). If no law were laid down, he says, to condemn the way of wickedness, evil would become powerless. For through the law it is all but provoked into strength. In some people the sting of pleasure will press with less force when no one rebukes it; it is all but blunted, charmed by the wide freedom it is given. For where there is nothing at all to resist, there the urge to contend surely lies idle as well. Sin, then, is dead when the law does not declare what must be done.

The guide into the mysteries says that he once lived without the law, and then, when the commandment came, he insists that sin came back to life, while he himself died (Romans 7:9–10). In these words he frames the argument in his own person, but I think he wishes to show something like this. It is agreed that even sinning in ignorance is liable to judgment. But that the punishment will be heavier for those who know, the Savior has made fully certain when he says, “The one who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47–48). It is agreed, then, that it is better to sin in ignorance than with knowledge of the laws. But suppose someone has come under the law after once living his life outside the law, and then, having chosen to disregard its decrees, has been convicted on a charge of sin and has fallen […]

ἔστησε ταῖς τριόδοις, ἐμφανῆ καθιστὰς τοῖς οὖσι τὰ μεταξὺ, οὐχ ἵνα πάλιν αὐτοῖς
περιπταίωσιν, ἀλλ' ἵνα μᾶλλον ὑπερφέροιντο καὶ ἀπαλλάττοιντο τοῦ κακοῦ· ἆρα οὖν
ἠδίκησε τὸ φῶς, ὅτι παρέδειξε τὸ λυποῦν; ἢ μᾶλλον ἐκεῖνό φαμεν, ὡς πλείστην ὅσην
αὐτοῖς ἐνεποίει τὴν ὄνησιν, ἀπετέλει δὲ καὶ ἀσφαλεστέρους; ἀλλ' οἶμαι τοῦτό ἐστιν
οὐδενὶ τῶν ὄντων ἀσυμφανές. ὅτε τοίνυν ὄντες ἁμαρτωλοὶ, πλείστοις τε ὅσοις
ἐγκλήμασι περιπταίοντες, ἐγνώκαμεν διὰ τοῦ νόμου τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, οὐχ ἁμαρτία μᾶλλον
ὁ νόμος νοοῖτ' ἂν εἰκότως ἢ λέγοιτο, πολλοῦ γε καὶ δεῖ, παραδεικτικὸς δὲ μᾶλλον τῆς
ἁμαρτίας, ὡς ἔφην. Τήν τε γὰρ ἐπιθυμίαν οὐκ ᾔδειν, εἰ μὴ ὁ νόμος οὐκ ἐπιθυ μήσεις
ἔλεγεν. ἀφορμὴν δὲ λαβοῦσα ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς κατειργάσατο ἐν ἐμοὶ πᾶσαν
ἐπιθυμίαν. Καὶ τὸ τῆς ἡμετέρας φύσεως ἀδρανὲς παρεισάγει, ὅτι δοθεὶς ὁ νόμος εἰς

10

ὄνησιν, ἐπεβούλευσεν ἀδοκήτως, ὡς καὶ τοῖς τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν ἀσθενοῦσι τοῦ ἡλίου τὸ
φῶς. ὅταν οὖν λέγῃ ἀφορμὴν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις τρόπον τινὰ τὴν ἐντολὴν γεγενῆσθαι,
μηδεὶς κατηγορεῖν αὐτὸν οἰέσθω τοῦ νόμου, ἀλλὰ 198 κατακεκραγέναι μᾶλλον τῆς ἐν
ἡμῖν ἀσθενείας· ἀνθ' ὧν ἐχρῆν ἀνακόπτεσθαι διὰ τοῦ νόμου, διὰ τούτων εἰς τὰ χείρω
παροτρυνομένους. ἡ γὰρ ἀνθρώπου διάνοια τὸ φιλόκενον ἀεὶ πρὸς ἐπιθυμίας νοσεῖ. καὶ
ὁ μὲν ποιῶν τὰς ἐπιθυμίας, ὡς θέλει ζῇ, ἀνενόχλητος ὤν· ὁ δὲ ἀνακόπτων αὐτὰς,
ἀγριωτέραν εἰσδέχεται τὴν τῶν παθῶν ἔφοδον· καὶ τῶν μὲν προχείρων οὐδεὶς ἐπιθυμεῖ·
ὧν δὲ κωλύεταί τις ἐπιθυμεῖ. ὅθεν τοῦ νόμου κωλύσαντος τὸ βλάπτον, γέγονεν ἀφορμὴ
τοῖς ἀσθενεστέροις τοῦ πλέον αὐτοῦ ἐπιθυμεῖν.
Χωρὶς γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία νεκρά. Εἰ γὰρ μὴ κέοιτο, φησὶν, ὁ τὸν τῆς φαυλότητος
τρόπον καταδικάζων νόμος, ἀδρανὲς ἂν γένοιτο τὸ κακόν· κατερεθίζεται γὰρ μονονουχὶ
πρὸς ἰσχὺν διὰ τοῦ νόμου, καὶ ῥᾳθυμότερον μέν τισι τὸ τῆς ἡδονῆς ἐγκείσεται κέντρον,
ἐπιτιμῶντος αὐτῷ μηδενός· μόνον δὲ οὐχὶ καὶ ἀπαμβλύνεται τῷ τῆς ἐξουσίας πλάτει
γοητευόμενον· οὗ γὰρ ὅλως τὸ ἀντιστατοῦν οὐδὲν, ἐκεῖ που πάντως ἀργεῖ καὶ τὸ
φιλόνεικον. νεκρὰ τοιγαροῦν ἡ ἁμαρτία, νόμου τὸ πρακτέον μὴ διαγορεύοντος·
ἐζηκέναι δέ φησιν ὁ μυσταγωγὸς χωρὶς νόμου ποτέ· εἶτα τῆς ἐντολῆς ἐλθούσης,
ἀναβιῶναι μὲν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, τεθνάναι γεμὴν ἑαυτὸν διισχυρίζεται. Καὶ σχηματίζει μὲν
ἐν τούτοις ἐφ' ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον· οἶμαι δὲ ἔγωγε τοιοῦτόν τι βούλεσθαι δηλοῦν αὐτόν·
ὑπὸ δίκην μὲν γὰρ ὁμολογουμένως ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ πλημμελεῖν· ἔσται δὲ ὅτι
φορτικωτέρα τοῖς εἰδόσιν ἡ κόλασις, πεπληροφόρηκεν ὁ Σωτὴρ λέγων Ὁ εἰδὼς τὸ
θέλημα τοῦ κυρίου αὐτοῦ, καὶ μὴ ποιήσας, δαρήσεται πολλάς· ὁ δὲ μὴ 199 εἰδὼς, καὶ μὴ
ποιήσας, δαρήσεται ὀλίγας. οὐκοῦν ἄμεινον ὁμολογουμένως τὸ ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ πλημμελεῖν,
ἢ τὸ ἐν εἰδήσει νόμων. εἰ δὲ δή τις γέγονεν ὑπὸ νόμον, τὴν ἔξω νόμου ποτὲ διαζήσας
ζωὴν, εἶτα τῶν τεθεσπισμένων ἀφειδεῖν ᾑρημένος, ἥλω γραφῇ ἁμαρτίας καὶ πέπτωκεν
reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Title said the law 'does not cause' sin, but the section itself says the commandment became an occasion for desire; Cyril's point is that the law is not sin but points it out (παραδεικτικὸς τῆς ἁμαρτίας). ἀφειδεῖν τῶν τεθεσπισμένων is 'disregard the decrees', not the stronger 'treat with contempt'. American spelling (offenses, Savior) to match this book's other rows and the u05 staging. Rest checked clause by clause against the Greek: faithful.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).
The section opens mid-sentence: the subject ('someone, taking a torch') stands at the end of u04-open (δᾷδά τις λαβὼν ἐπ' αὐταῖς). The break is marked […].
The section ends mid-sentence (πέπτωκεν | ὑπὸ δίκην); 'under sentence' opens u04-rem-mid. The break is marked […].
The page number 10 and PG column number 198/199 in the source block are not translated. The line-break split ἐπιθυ μήσεις is read as ἐπιθυμήσεις.
ἐπιθυμία is rendered 'covetous desire' inside the Romans lemma, to keep the link with 'You shall not covet', and 'desire(s)' in Cyril's own comment.
ὁ μυσταγωγός ('the one who initiates into the mysteries') is Cyril's title for Paul; rendered 'the guide into the mysteries'.
τὸ φιλόκενον ('love of the empty/vain') is printed so; φιλόκαινον ('love of novelty') would also fit the context, but the printed reading is kept.
Cyril's form of Luke 12:48 ('the one who does not know and does not do it') differs from the Gospel text ('did what deserved blows'); his wording is translated as printed.
ἐπεβούλευσεν ('plotted against') is rendered 'turned against us'; the object is implied.
